narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 25, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling that this was the main reason the model saw a higher risk of not passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.30 it is slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model viewed this as a modest positive factor that pulled the prediction somewhat toward passing. However, this helpful effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your LSAT score.

Your third-year grades also nudged the outcome slightly toward passing. Being in the fourth decile is a bit below the 5.79 average of accepted students, yet the model still treated this as a small positive signal overall.

In short, the low LSAT score outweighed your solid GPA and decent class ranking, tipping the model just over the threshold for rejection.

What you should do next is retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score. Improving that single area would likely change the prediction and give your application a much stronger chance of acceptance.
